__README__: Migrations merged BEFORE scripts/migration-lint.mjs existed, with a written reason each.
RECORDED, not suppressed. The measured verdict of MI-001 over the 91 migrations on main at
e5d3c4fd is 13 findings across 3 migrations, every one listed below with what it is. Every
one is ACCEPTED — this unit ships no rule that fires on a live defect.
TWO LIVE DEFECTS ARE KNOWN ON MERGED MIGRATIONS AND NEITHER HAS A BACKSTOP HERE:
20270225000000_phase4_t3_correction3:169 is caught only by MI-002, and
20270920000000_decision_option_kinds:273 only by MI-003. Both rules are deferred, so neither
defect has an entry below and nothing in CI fires on either. They are recorded in
docs/MIGRATION_INVARIANTS.md with the head that carries each corrected rule. Deferring a
rule did not unfind its defect; it removed the alarm.
EVERY COUNT HERE IS PER SITE. Codex findings F2/F3 against head c6e9ff17 were the same defect:
each rule asked its question of the FILE, so one satisfied site discharged every other and one
correct guard shielded an arbitrary number of defective neighbours. MI-001 alone went from 4
findings to 13 once that was corrected — the two sites in the B1 migration were INVISIBLE
before it, excused by a third section's pg_get_triggerdef. That is the rule working.
MI-000, MI-003 and MI-004 are deferred to the follow-on unit; their corrected implementations,
fixtures and this ledger's previous MI-003 and MI-004 entries are committed on this branch and
recorded in docs/MIGRATION_INVARIANTS.md. Nothing was deferred silently.
A NEW migration cannot join this list without an owner editing this file, which is the point:
the cost of an exception is a visible diff, not silence. Two tests keep it honest — every entry
must name a real migration and rule with a checkable reason, and none may be DEAD.

20270225000000_phase4_t3_correction3.MI-001: ACCEPTED — 10 sites, up from 3 before the per-site binding. Every one resolves a catalog object by name inside a guard that refuses, and none reads a definition IN THAT GUARD. The comparison lives in the compiled `t3c seals` verifier (dist/.../t3c.cli.js), which apps/api/scripts/migrate.sh invokes on the deploy success path at line 120 and again after baseline at line 291, so a wrong definition IS refused — just not by this file. The migration's own guards are a presence census in front of that verifier rather than the verifier itself.

20270920000000_decision_option_kinds.MI-001: ACCEPTED — 1 site. Line 552 resolves a trigger by tgname inside a guard that refuses, without comparing pg_get_triggerdef. The consequence here is a FAILED APPLY rather than a false clearance: the guard runs during the migration's own apply, when the trigger it names has just been created by this same file, so a same-named foreign object means the apply aborts. A wrong definition is not silently accepted; the migration refuses to finish.

20270930000000_schedule_dependency_graph.MI-001: ACCEPTED — 2 sites (sections 1 and 9, both pg_trigger), and both were INVISIBLE before the per-site binding because section 8's pg_get_triggerdef excused them at file scope. Accepted on the merged evidence: section 8 stands between them and refuses a wrong definition, and section 9 enumerates every component the deparse renders for five triggers that carry no WHEN clause and no arguments, so the name plus the enumerated components is the whole definition for those five. The finding is that sections 1 and 9 depend on section 8 having run, which is true in this file and is not a property the linter can see.
